reference.source: Williams Obstetrics / Novak's Gynecology / Campbell-Walsh Urology
clinicalPearls: Shoulder dystocia is failure of the shoulders to deliver after the head, caused by impaction of the anterior shoulder behind the maternal pubic symphysis, and is a time-critical obstetric emergency
The warning sign is the turtle sign, where the delivered head retracts tightly against the perineum, and failure of restitution and of routine gentle traction to deliver the body

Risk factors include fetal macrosomia, maternal diabetes, previous shoulder dystocia, obesity, prolonged labour, and instrumental delivery, but many cases occur without identifiable risk factors so all birth attendants must be prepared
Management follows a structured sequence: call for help, avoid the harmful HELPER pitfalls, and apply the McRoberts manoeuvre with suprapubic pressure as first-line steps
If initial measures fail, internal rotational manoeuvres (such as delivery of the posterior arm or rotational techniques) are used, and the mother should not be pushed while shoulders are impacted
Fundal pressure must be avoided because it worsens impaction and increases the risk of uterine rupture
Excessive or downward traction on the fetal head is the main modifiable cause of brachial plexus injury and should be avoided
Complications include brachial plexus palsy (Erb palsy), clavicular or humeral fracture, hypoxic injury from delay, and maternal postpartum haemorrhage and perineal trauma
Accurate contemporaneous documentation of the sequence, manoeuvres, timings, and personnel is essential given the medicolegal significance
reference.pathophysiology: After the fetal head delivers, the shoulders normally rotate into the wider oblique diameter of the pelvis. In shoulder dystocia the anterior shoulder fails to rotate and becomes wedged above the pubic symphysis (or, less commonly, the posterior shoulder impacts on the sacral promontory). Because the fetus can no longer descend, the umbilical cord is compressed within the pelvis and placental gas exchange is impaired, so fetal hypoxia and acidosis progress with time. Rotational manoeuvres and delivery of the posterior arm work by reducing the shoulder-to-shoulder (bisacromial) diameter or moving it into a larger pelvic diameter, freeing the impaction.
additionalDifferentials: Difficulty from a tight nuchal cord without true shoulder impaction
Fetal anomalies causing enlarged trunk or abdomen (e.g. large abdominal mass, hydrops)
Uterine or contraction abnormality causing prolonged second stage
additionalInvestigations: Immediate clinical recognition rather than investigation is the priority in the acute event
Neonatal assessment of the arms, clavicles, and neurology for brachial plexus injury or fracture after delivery
Cord blood gas analysis to document the degree of any acidosis
Maternal assessment for postpartum haemorrhage and perineal or anal sphincter trauma
Antenatal estimation of fetal weight and screening for diabetes in at-risk pregnancies
redFlags: OBSTETRIC EMERGENCY: head delivered with turtle sign and shoulders not delivering despite routine traction, requiring immediate structured manoeuvres
Prolonged head-to-body delivery interval with rising risk of hypoxic-ischaemic injury
Signs of neonatal brachial plexus injury or limb fracture after delivery
Maternal postpartum haemorrhage or severe perineal and anal sphincter trauma
Use of fundal pressure or excessive head traction indicating unsafe technique
reference.prognosis: Most shoulder dystocias are relieved with recognised manoeuvres and the majority of infants have no lasting harm. Brachial plexus injuries are the commonest fetal complication and most resolve within the first year, though a minority are permanent. Prolonged impaction risks hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy or death. Women who have had shoulder dystocia have an increased recurrence risk in subsequent pregnancies.
pitfalls: Applying fundal pressure, which worsens impaction and can cause uterine rupture
Using excessive downward traction on the head, the leading cause of brachial plexus injury
Encouraging maternal pushing while the shoulder remains impacted
Failing to summon senior and neonatal help early
Poor documentation of manoeuvres and timings in a medicolegally significant event
management: Immediate declaration of the emergency and summoning of senior help, including additional midwifery, obstetric, neonatal and anaesthetic staff
McRoberts manoeuvre with suprapubic pressure as the first-line step to free the impacted anterior shoulder
Avoidance of fundal pressure and of excessive downward traction, and instruction to the mother to stop pushing while the shoulders are impacted
Internal rotational manoeuvres and delivery of the posterior arm if first-line measures fail, aided by episiotomy to create room
Last-resort manoeuvres including the all-fours position and, if all else fails, cleidotomy, symphysiotomy or cephalic replacement
Neonatal assessment for brachial plexus injury and clavicular or humeral fracture, with cord blood gas analysis to document any acidosis
Maternal assessment for postpartum haemorrhage and perineal or anal sphincter trauma, with contemporaneous documentation and debrief
